summary: Chinese has no articles. A bare noun is read as known or new from context and from its place: a noun before the verb is usually something known (书在这里 ‘the book is here’, 钥匙不在这里 ‘the keys aren’t here’). To introduce one new thing, Chinese can use 一 + measure word (这是一本书 ‘this is a book’), but often a bare noun is enough (这是书). To point at a known thing, 这 / 那 + measure word (这本书 ‘this book’). From S06 on, 有 adds the other half: 这里有书 ‘there is a book here’ — a new thing after the verb.

blocks.caption: Known and new things — without articles

blocks.title: 这 points — it is not an article
blocks.text: 这本书 means ‘this book’. A thing that is simply known takes no word at all: 书在这里 ‘the book is here’.

notes.text: ‘This book’ is 这本书, but ‘the book’ is just 书: never translate ‘the’ with 这.
der / die / das is not 这: das Buch ist hier is 书在这里; 这本书 is dieses Buch.
le livre is just 书 (书在这里 ‘le livre est ici’); 这本书 is ce livre(-ci).
el libro is just 书 (书在这里); 这本书 is este libro.
il libro is just 书 (书在这里); 这本书 is questo libro.
o livro is just 书 (书在这里); 这本书 is este livro.
το βιβλίο is just 书 (书在这里); 这本书 is αυτό το βιβλίο.
The ending of libri is not 这: libri është këtu is 书在这里; 这本书 is ky libër.

blocks.title: Don’t add 一个 to every new noun
blocks.text: 这是书 ‘this is a book’ and 我是学生 ‘I am a student’ need nothing; 一 + measure word stresses ‘one’ or introduces something new.

notes.text: ‘I am a student’ is 我是学生: the English ‘a’ needs no counterpart, and 一个 means ‘one’ or brings in something new.
ein / eine has no obligatory counterpart: es ist ein Buch ~ 这是书 or 这是一本书, ich bin Lehrer ~ 我是老师.
un / une has no obligatory counterpart: c’est un livre ~ 这是书 or 这是一本书, je suis étudiant ~ 我是学生.
un / una has no obligatory counterpart: es un libro ~ 这是书 or 这是一本书, soy estudiante ~ 我是学生.
un / una has no obligatory counterpart: è un libro ~ 这是书 or 这是一本书, sono studente ~ 我是学生.
um / uma has no obligatory counterpart: é um livro ~ 这是书 or 这是一本书, sou estudante ~ 我是学生.
ένας / μία / ένα has no obligatory counterpart: είναι ένα βιβλίο ~ 这是书 or 这是一本书, είμαι φοιτητής ~ 我是学生.
një has no obligatory counterpart: është një libër ~ 这是书 or 这是一本书, jam student ~ 我是学生.

items.title: New
points: 一 + measure word, or after 有 (S06)

askYourself: Is the thing already known to both speakers? → a bare noun, usually before the verb: 书在这里.
Am I introducing one new thing? → 一 + measure word (这是一本书) — or just the bare noun.
Must I point at it? → 这 / 那 + measure word.
Am I looking for a word that marks a thing as known? → there is none: usually the bare noun.

traps: Do not use 这 just to mark a known thing: 这 means ‘this’ and points.
Do not add 一个 to every single new noun: 我是老师, not necessarily 我是一个老师.
A known thing goes before the verb: 钥匙在这里 ‘the keys are here’ — 这里有钥匙 (S06) means ‘there are keys here’.

quiz.q: How does Chinese mark a thing as known (definite)?
quiz.why: Chinese has no article; 这 is ‘this’.
A bare noun before the verb is a known thing.
一 + measure word introduces one new thing.

quiz.q: Which word marks 钥匙 as known in 钥匙不在这里 (‘the keys aren’t here’)?
quiz.why: 钥匙 alone, before the verb, is understood as ‘the keys’.

notes.text: Greek uses ο / η / το for known things and ένας / μία / ένα for new ones; Chinese has no ‘the’, and 一 + measure word is the counterpart of ένας. Position does the rest: a known thing stands before the verb (书在这里).
Russian has no articles either and uses word order the same way: Книга на столе (the book) vs На столе книга (a book) — exactly 书在桌子上 vs 桌子上有一本书.
Spanish el / la / un / una come with nearly every noun; Chinese has none — 一 + measure word only when ‘one’ or a new thing matters.
English the / a are obligatory; Chinese has neither. Word order does the work of ‘the’: a known thing before the verb (书在这里 ‘the book is here’), a new thing after 有 (这里有书 ‘there is a book here’).
French le / la / les / un / une / du are obligatory; Chinese has none — 我喝咖啡 is je bois du café and je bois le café alike.
German der / ein carry gender and case; Chinese has no article at all, and 一 + measure word appears only when ‘one’ matters.
Hindi has no definite article either and uses एक like 一 + measure word for something new; Hindi marks a known object with को, which Chinese does not need.
Persian has no ‘the’; a new thing gets -i or yek (ketābi ‘a book’), a known object rā. Chinese has only 一 + measure word for ‘a’ and nothing for ‘the’ or a known object.
Marathi has no articles; एक ‘one’ introduces a new thing, like Chinese 一 + measure word.
Arabic al- makes a noun definite and -un (tanwīn) often marks it indefinite; Chinese marks neither — position and 这 / 那 do the work.
Hebrew ha- marks a known noun and repeats on its adjective (ha-bayit ha-gadol); Chinese has no article: 大房子 is ‘a big house’ or ‘the big house’ by context.
Turkish has no ‘the’ and uses bir for ‘a’ — exactly 一 + measure word. A known object takes -ı in Turkish (kitabı okudum); Chinese marks it with nothing.
Japanese has no articles either; the topic particle は marks known things, a role Chinese gives to the start of the sentence.
Korean has no articles; 은 / 는 marks a known topic, which Chinese shows by putting it first.
Finnish has no articles and uses word order like Chinese: Kirja on pöydällä ‘the book is on the table’ vs Pöydällä on kirja ‘there is a book on the table’.
Hungarian has a / az and egy, like an article system; Chinese has neither — position does the work of ‘the’, and 一 + measure word that of ‘a’.
Swahili has no articles; demonstratives or context make a noun definite, as in Chinese.
Luganda has no article words; as in Chinese, context and position decide whether a noun is known.
Vietnamese has no definite article either; một ‘one’ + classifier introduces a new thing (một cái bàn), just like 一张桌子.
Inuktitut has no articles; neither has Chinese.

Italian il / la / lo / un / una and the partitive del come with nearly every noun; Chinese has none — 我喝咖啡 is bevo il caffè and bevo del caffè alike. 一 + measure word appears only when ‘one’ or a new thing matters.

Albanian marks a known noun with an ending (libër → libri ‘the book’) and a new one with një (një libër); Chinese has neither: 书在这里 ‘the book is here’. 一 + measure word is the counterpart of një, and position does the work of the ending.
Portuguese o / a / um / uma come with nearly every noun, even before names and possessives (o João, o meu livro); Chinese has none: 书, 我的书 — 一 + measure word only when ‘one’ or a new thing matters.

If your language has articles that agree in gender, number or case, Chinese has none at all: a bare noun is known or new by context and position (书在这里 / 这里有书), and 一 + measure word is not an obligatory article.
If your language has no definite article and marks a known object with a case ending, Chinese marks neither: position does the work — a known thing before the verb (书在这里), a new one after 有 (这里有书).
If your language has no articles and uses ‘one’ + classifier for a new thing, Chinese does exactly that (一本书); a bare noun before the verb is a known thing (书在这里).
If your language has no articles, neither has Chinese; known and new are shown by position: 书在这里 (known), 这里有书 (new).

If your language marks a known noun with a definite prefix (repeated on its adjective), Chinese marks nothing: 大房子 is ‘a big house’ or ‘the big house’ by context, and a known thing tends to stand before the verb (书在这里).

seeAlso.note: German der / die / das and ein / eine also show gender and case; Chinese has no article at all.
Arabic marks ‘the’ with al- (al-kitāb) and ‘a’ with -un (kitābun); Chinese uses word order and context.
Hebrew marks a known noun with ha- and a new one with nothing — like Chinese for new things, but Chinese has no mark for known ones either.
